articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $4.2 Million Tourism Contract Renewed Without Competitive Bid
articles.dek: The county commission quietly extended Visit Pensacola's management agreement last month. Three commissioners have received campaign contributions from tourism industry PACs.
brief: Escambia County commissioners voted 4-1 on May 14 to extend Visit Pensacola's tourism management contract for three years without soliciting competing proposals
The renewed agreement totals $4.2 million annually in bed tax revenue, with no performance benchmarks tied to funding levels
Campaign finance records show three commissioners who voted yes received a combined $18,500 from tourism industry PACs since 2024
articles.body:
The vote took forty-three seconds. No discussion. No questions from the dais. On May 14, four Escambia County commissioners extended a $4.2 million annual contract to Visit Pensacola, the nonprofit that has managed the county's tourism marketing since 2012.

Commissioner Doug Underhill cast the lone dissenting vote. He did not explain his opposition during the meeting. The item appeared on the consent agenda—a batch of routine matters approved in a single motion.

Visit Pensacola's previous three-year contract expired June 30. The organization operates as the county's designated tourism development agency, funded almost entirely by the Tourist Development Tax, a 5% levy on short-term lodging. The renewed agreement runs through June 2029.

County records obtained through a public records request show no evidence that staff solicited proposals from other destination marketing organizations before the renewal. Escambia County Purchasing Director Maria Santos confirmed in an email that competitive bidding was not required.

"Professional services contracts of this nature fall under an exemption in Florida Statute 287.057," Santos wrote. "The Board has discretion to negotiate directly with the existing provider."

Campaign Contributions

Campaign finance records filed with the Escambia County Supervisor of Elections show connections between the commissioners who approved the contract and tourism industry interests.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh received $7,500 from the Florida Restaurant and Lodging Association PAC between January 2024 and March 2026. Commissioner Steven Barry received $6,000 from the same PAC over the same period. Commissioner Lumon May received $5,000 from Visit Florida's political committee in 2024.

All three voted to approve the contract extension. Commissioner Mike Kohler, who also voted yes, received no tourism-related PAC contributions during that period, according to available records.

Bergosh did not respond to requests for comment. Barry, reached by phone, said the contributions played no role in his vote.

"Visit Pensacola has done a good job for this county," Barry said. "That's why I supported the renewal. Campaign donations don't factor into my decisions on contracts."

May's office declined to comment.

Contract Terms

The renewed agreement guarantees Visit Pensacola $4.2 million annually from bed tax collections—the same funding level as the previous contract. The organization receives 40% of all Tourist Development Tax revenue, with remaining funds split between beach renourishment, sports marketing, and capital projects.

Unlike tourism contracts in neighboring Santa Rosa County, Escambia's agreement includes no performance benchmarks tied to funding. Santa Rosa's deal with its destination marketing organization requires measurable increases in hotel occupancy rates, with funding adjustments if targets are missed.

Visit Pensacola CEO Darien Schaefer defended the organization's track record in an interview.

"We've generated over $2.8 billion in visitor spending since 2020," Schaefer said. "Our metrics speak for themselves. The commission has confidence in our work because we deliver results."

Schaefer said the organization welcomed accountability measures but noted the commission had not requested any.

"If they want benchmarks, we're happy to discuss that," he said. "That conversation hasn't happened."

Previous Scrutiny

Visit Pensacola's contract has drawn criticism before. In 2019, a county audit found the organization spent $47,000 on out-of-state travel for staff and board members over two years, including trips to conferences in Las Vegas and San Diego. The audit recommended tighter expense reporting.

Visit Pensacola implemented new travel policies following the audit. Schaefer said current spending adheres to those guidelines.

The organization's board includes representatives from major hotels, attractions, and restaurants in the county. Board meeting minutes are not posted on Visit Pensacola's website. Schaefer said minutes are available upon request.

What Happens Next

The renewed contract takes effect July 1. It includes a clause allowing either party to terminate with 180 days' notice.

Underhill, the dissenting commissioner, did not return calls seeking comment. His office provided no statement explaining his vote.

The next scheduled discussion of tourism funding is set for the commission's September budget workshop. Bed tax revenue projections for fiscal year 2027 will be presented at that meeting.

Visit Pensacola's annual report, required under the contract, is due to the commission by October 15.

articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Who Owns Pensacola Beach? A Land Lease Audit Reveals 47 Parcels With Expired Terms
articles.dek: Santa Rosa Island Authority records show dozens of commercial leaseholders operating month-to-month while negotiations stall. Some haven't paid increased rates in three years.
brief: 47 commercial parcels on Pensacola Beach are operating on expired leases, with some leaseholders month-to-month for over three years
The Santa Rosa Island Authority is owed an estimated $2.3 million in deferred rate increases that were never collected
Legal ambiguity over Escambia County's deed restrictions complicates renewal negotiations and any potential enforcement
articles.body:
The fence went up around the empty lot at 715 Via de Luna in March. No permit posted. No contractor sign. Just chain-link and silence where a beach bar called The Sandbar used to stand until a kitchen fire gutted it in 2022.

The lot's leaseholder, a Destin-based LLC called Emerald Hospitality Group, hasn't rebuilt. Hasn't announced plans. Hasn't responded to three certified letters from the Santa Rosa Island Authority requesting a meeting about the property's future.

The company also hasn't paid the rate increase that took effect when its 25-year lease expired in September 2023. It's not alone.

A Flightline audit of SRIA property records obtained through public records requests reveals that 47 commercial parcels on Pensacola Beach are currently operating on expired lease terms. Some have been month-to-month for more than three years. Together, these leaseholders owe an estimated $2.3 million in rate increases that the authority approved but never collected.

The island that nobody owns

Pensacola Beach exists in a legal gray zone that confuses even longtime residents. The land belongs to Escambia County. The county leases it to the SRIA. The SRIA subleases individual parcels to businesses and residents. Nobody owns anything outright. Everybody pays rent to somebody.

This arrangement dates to 1947, when the state of Florida transferred Santa Rosa Island to Escambia County with a deed restriction requiring the land be used for "public purposes." The county created the SRIA to manage development while theoretically preserving public access.

Commercial leases typically run 25 or 30 years. When they expire, the SRIA is supposed to negotiate renewals at current market rates. The problem, according to SRIA records and interviews with three current board members, is that nobody can agree on what market rate means for land you can't actually buy.

"We're not comparing apples to apples," said SRIA board member Janet Kirkland during a February meeting. "There is no comparable market. This is the only public beach in Florida structured this way."

The backlog builds

The 47 expired leases represent about 22% of the commercial parcels on the island. They include restaurants, hotels, retail shops and service businesses. The Flightline reviewed lease files for 31 of these properties. The patterns were consistent:

Standard lease language requires leaseholders to begin renewal negotiations 18 months before expiration. Of the 31 files reviewed, only seven showed evidence of timely negotiation requests from leaseholders. Nine showed no renewal correspondence at all.

When the SRIA did propose new terms, leaseholders frequently contested the rate increases. The authority's 2021 rate study recommended increases ranging from 15% to 40% depending on location and property use. Many leaseholders called these figures arbitrary.

"They pulled numbers out of the air," said Marcus Webb, who operates a jet ski rental business near the fishing pier. His lease expired in 2024. He's been paying his old rate while disputing the new one. "Show me the comps. There are no comps. It's whatever they decide to charge."

The SRIA declined to make executive director Tom Campanella available for an interview. In a written statement, the authority said it "continues to work in good faith with all leaseholders to reach mutually acceptable renewal terms" and that "enforcement actions remain available but are not the preferred resolution method."

Enforcement? What enforcement?

The SRIA's enforcement options are limited and legally untested. Standard lease language allows the authority to terminate for non-payment or material breach. But expired-term operation isn't clearly defined as either.

Escambia County Attorney Alison Rogers told commissioners in a closed session last October—minutes of which were later released through a public records request—that any termination attempt would likely trigger litigation. The deed restrictions complicate matters further.

"The county's position is that the land must remain available for public purposes," Rogers wrote in a memo to commissioners. "Whether that obligation transfers to SRIA enforcement actions is an open question. We would be litigating first impression issues."

Translation: Nobody wants to be the test case.

The result is a standoff. Leaseholders keep operating and paying old rates. The SRIA keeps sending letters. The backlog grows.

Following the money

The $2.3 million in deferred rate increases isn't a precise figure. It's an estimate based on the difference between what expired-lease holders are paying and what they would pay under the 2021 rate study recommendations, multiplied by the months since expiration.

Some of that money may never be recoverable. Lease language is ambiguous about whether rate increases apply retroactively once a renewal is signed or only going forward. The SRIA has taken both positions in different negotiations, according to correspondence reviewed by The Flightline.

What's clear is that the authority's budget feels the squeeze. SRIA revenues fund beach maintenance, lifeguards, public parking and the trolley system. The 2026 budget projects a $400,000 shortfall that staff attributed partly to "lease revenue underperformance."

Board member David Chen proposed a resolution in April that would have set a hard deadline: negotiate within 90 days or face formal breach proceedings. It failed 3-2. The opposing votes cited litigation risk and "relationship preservation" with business owners.

"We're a small island," said board member Patricia Simmons, who voted against the resolution. "These are our neighbors. We see them at Publix. There has to be a better way than lawyers."

The empty lot

Back at 715 Via de Luna, the fence has acquired a patina of salt and rust. Someone taped a handwritten sign to it in April: "WHAT'S GOING IN HERE?" The question remains unanswered.

Emerald Hospitality Group's registered agent in Tallahassee confirmed the company still exists but declined to comment on its plans for the property. SRIA records show the lot's lease payments are current at the pre-expiration rate of $2,847 per month. The post-expiration rate would be $4,100.

The lot sits 200 feet from the Gulf. On a clear day, you can see the condos on Perdido Key from the vacant concrete pad where the kitchen used to be.

It's prime real estate. Sort of. If anyone could actually own it.

This analysis is based on SRIA lease records, board meeting minutes, county commission documents and interviews with board members and leaseholders obtained between March and May 2026. Requests for additional records regarding enforcement discussions are pending.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's Quiet Housing Crisis: 200 Navy Families on Waitlist as Privatized Units Sit Vacant
articles.dek: A mold remediation backlog has left military housing units empty while junior enlisted families pay Pensacola rents that have jumped 34 percent since 2022.
brief: More than 200 Navy families are on a waitlist for privatized housing at NAS Pensacola while dozens of units remain vacant due to mold remediation delays.
Junior enlisted sailors with families face off-base rents averaging $1,847 per month—often exceeding their Basic Allowance for Housing by $300 or more.
The housing contractor, Balfour Beatty Communities, cites supply chain issues and a regional shortage of certified mold remediation crews.
articles.body:
The white two-story duplex at 142 Radford Boulevard looks move-in ready from the street. Fresh mulch rings the live oak out front. The lawn is trimmed. A FOR RENT sign from Balfour Beatty Communities hangs in the window.

But the front door has been locked since February 2025. Black mold blooms behind the drywall in both bedrooms. The HVAC system tested positive for aspergillus spores in November. No one has touched it since.

Fifteen months of vacancy. One of 47 units sitting empty across NAS Pensacola's privatized family housing inventory while 203 families wait for a place to live.

"I drive past these houses every day on my way to work," said Aviation Electronics Technician Second Class Marcus Okonkwo, who has been on the waitlist since August 2025. "They told me six to eight weeks when I signed up. It's been ten months."

Okonkwo, his wife and their two children rent a three-bedroom apartment in Warrington. The rent is $1,925 a month. His Basic Allowance for Housing—the monthly stipend the Navy provides for off-base living—is $1,641.

The math doesn't work. He picks up weekend shifts detailing cars at a lot on Navy Boulevard.

The Mold Problem Nobody Budgeted For

Balfour Beatty Communities has managed privatized military housing at NAS Pensacola since 2005, part of a 50-year contract worth an estimated $2.1 billion. Under the Military Housing Privatization Initiative, the company owns the housing units and collects BAH payments directly from residents. In exchange, it maintains the properties and keeps them habitable.

That arrangement worked well enough when the housing stock was newer and the Gulf Coast construction labor market wasn't stretched thin. Neither condition holds anymore.

The mold crisis started accelerating in 2023. Hurricane Sally's flooding in 2020 had damaged drainage systems across the base. Repairs were delayed by pandemic supply chain issues. By the time crews got to some units, moisture had been trapped in wall cavities for three years.

A Navy Inspector General report from March 2025 found that 23 percent of family housing units at NAS Pensacola had documented mold issues requiring professional remediation. The report noted that Balfour Beatty had addressed complaints in common areas and visible surfaces but had not consistently tested for mold behind walls or in HVAC systems.

"The pattern we observed was reactive rather than proactive," the report stated. "Remediation often occurred only after residents reported respiratory symptoms or visible growth."

Balfour Beatty spokesperson Jennifer Callahan said in a written statement that the company has "invested more than $4.2 million in mold remediation at NAS Pensacola since 2023" and has "prioritized the health and safety of our residents throughout this process."

But the company has struggled to find contractors. Certified mold remediation crews in the Pensacola area are booked months out, handling a backlog of post-hurricane work from both Hurricane Sally and Hurricane Ida. Balfour Beatty has brought in crews from Mobile and Biloxi, but housing them adds cost and complexity.

"We are working as quickly as the regional labor market allows," Callahan wrote. "We share the frustration of families waiting for housing."

The Rent Squeeze

While military families wait, Pensacola's rental market keeps climbing.

Median rent for a three-bedroom unit in Escambia County hit $1,847 in April 2026, according to Zillow data. That's up 34 percent from $1,378 in April 2022. The spike tracks with Pensacola's broader housing crunch—population growth, short-term rental conversions and construction costs that have priced out new apartment development.

BAH rates, set annually by the Department of Defense based on local housing surveys, have not kept pace. The 2026 BAH for an E-5 with dependents stationed at NAS Pensacola is $1,641 per month. An E-4 with dependents receives $1,557.

The gap between BAH and actual rent—what housing advocates call the "out-of-pocket burden"—averages $206 to $290 per month for junior enlisted families in the Pensacola area, according to an analysis by the Military Family Advisory Network.

"That's grocery money," said Tanya Williamson, MFAN's Southeast regional director. "That's the difference between making it and not making it for a family with young kids."

Senior enlisted and officer families face less strain. A Chief Petty Officer with dependents receives $2,094 in BAH. A lieutenant commander gets $2,541. The gap narrows or disappears entirely.

"It's the junior sailors who get squeezed," said Master Chief Petty Officer Darnell Hayes, the command master chief for Naval Air Technical Training Center. "They're the ones we're trying to retain, and we're making it hard on them."

No Easy Answers

Captain Lydia Chen, commanding officer of NAS Pensacola, said the base is aware of the housing pressure and has raised concerns with Navy Region Southeast.

"We don't control Balfour Beatty's timeline, and we don't set BAH rates," Chen said in an interview. "What we can do is advocate for our people, and we are."

Chen said the base has connected some families with emergency financial assistance through Navy-Marine Corps Relief Society and has worked with local landlords to identify apartments willing to rent at BAH rates. But those units tend to be older, farther from base or in neighborhoods with higher crime rates.

"It's not a great answer," Chen acknowledged.

Meanwhile, the waitlist keeps growing. Petty Officer Second Class Aaliyah Freeman, a hospital corpsman at the Naval Hospital Pensacola clinic, added her name in March. She and her husband—also active duty, stationed at Corry Station—have a one-year-old daughter. They rent a two-bedroom in Ferry Pass for $1,650 a month, utilities not included.

"We're making it work," Freeman said. "But we're not saving anything. If something breaks, we're in trouble."

She checks the Balfour Beatty portal every week. The number ahead of her in line ticks down slowly. Some weeks it goes up—families transferring in from other duty stations, getting added to the queue.

"They tell you the military takes care of its own," Freeman said. "I'm still waiting to see that part."

What Comes Next

Balfour Beatty expects to complete remediation on 18 units by the end of July and another 15 by October. If that timeline holds, the waitlist could start moving by fall.

But the company has missed deadlines before. A batch of 12 units promised for January 2026 delivery didn't come online until April. Six are still awaiting final inspection.

Navy Region Southeast is conducting a review of all privatized housing contracts in Florida, a spokesperson confirmed. The review will assess contractor performance, maintenance backlogs and resident satisfaction. Results are expected in early 2027.

For families like the Okonkwos, that's another year and a half of waiting. Another year of rent checks that eat into grocery money. Another year of watching empty houses sit quiet on Radford Boulevard.

"I joined the Navy to build a life for my family," Okonkwo said. "Right now it feels like we're just trying to hold on."
